name: Dubnium

discovery.discoverer: Contested — claims by teams at Dubna, USSR and Berkeley, USA

occurrence: Does not occur naturally; produced only via particle accelerator fusion, atom by atom, decaying within seconds.
majorUses: No practical applications — pure superheavy-element research
safetyNotes: Intensely radioactive with half-lives measured in seconds to roughly an hour for its most stable known isotope.
notableCharacteristics: Named after Dubna, Russia, home of the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research, one of the two rival laboratories most responsible for discovering the superheavy elements.
ncertRelevance: named after a research institution's location
whyHere: Predicted to sit in Group 5 alongside tantalum and niobium, dubnium's expected chemistry (favouring a +5 oxidation state) follows directly from its position, though confirming this experimentally requires painstaking single-atom chemistry techniques.
didYouKnow: The 'Transfermium Wars' dispute over naming elements 104-109 between American and Soviet/Russian teams got so heated that IUPAC didn't issue final, internationally agreed names until 1997 — decades after some of these elements were first created.
genZNote: Named after a Russian research city and caught in a decades-long international naming feud. Chemistry has drama too, apparently.
